Leave
lēv
v. (to depart from; to let remain; to forsake — in Scripture the founding verb of marriage and the promise God gives to the fearful)
From Anglo-Saxon laefan, to let remain — causative of lifan, to remain. The English verb carries two nearly opposite senses that Scripture uses both of: to go away from, and to let stay.

Biblical Definition

Leave founds the institution of marriage: “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh” (Gen 2:24) — three verbs in order, and the order is not negotiable. A man leaves, then cleaves, then the two are one flesh; a household is established by a public departure from another household, and the Lord Jesus and Paul both cite the verse as the permanent charter of marriage. The word also carries the strongest negative promise in Scripture: “he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” (Heb 13:5) — and the writer produces it, remarkably, as the cure for covetousness, since a man who is certain of God's presence does not need to hoard. It governs the priority of reconciliation over ritual: “Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother” (Mat 5:24). And in the Psalter it becomes the great resurrection promise, quoted by Peter at Pentecost: “thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption” (Psa 16:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines leave as to withdraw or depart from, to forsake, to quit — and also as to suffer to remain, to permit without interposition.

expand to see more

LEAVE, v.t. To withdraw or depart from; to quit for a longer or shorter time indefinitely, or forever.

A man shall leave his father and his mother. Gen. ii.

2. To forsake; to desert; to abandon; to relinquish.

3. To suffer to remain; not to take or remove.

4. To have remaining at death; as, to leave a good name.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:24 — "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh."

Heb 13:5 — "Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee."

Mat 5:24 — "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift."

Psa 16:10 — "For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption."

Modern Corruption

Gen 2:24 is treated as a description of ancient custom rather than a creation ordinance, and the leaving clause is quietly dropped from a culture of unformed households.

expand to see more

The verse is the charter of marriage and both the Lord and the apostle treat it that way. Christ answers the divorce question by going behind Moses to it — “from the beginning it was not so” (Mat 19:8) — and Paul cites it in Eph 5:31 as the pattern of Christ and the church. That places marriage among the creation ordinances, given before the fall, for all mankind and not merely for the covenant community, and it forecloses the modern reading of marriage as an evolving social arrangement whose terms a society may set for itself. One man, one woman, leaving, cleaving, one flesh.

The neglected clause is the first one. Households are formed by leaving, and a marriage in which the primary loyalty of either party has not visibly transferred from parents to spouse has not fully begun. The corresponding modern failure is the indefinitely postponed household — men who never leave, in the sense of never assuming the weight of headship and provision, and marriages contracted without the public break that Gen 2:24 assumes. Heb 13:5 is the promise that makes the leaving possible: a man may let go of every other security because the One who says I will never leave thee does not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Anglo-Saxon laefan, to let remain; rendering Hebrew azab (H5800), to forsake or leave, and yathar (H3498), to leave over, and Greek kataleipo (G2641) and aphiemi (G863).

expand to see more

Hebrew azab (H5800) — to leave, forsake; the verb of Gen 2:24 and of the cry “why hast thou forsaken me” (Psa 22:1).

Hebrew dabaq (H1692) — to cleave, be glued to; the second verb of Gen 2:24, and the word used of Ruth cleaving unto Naomi.

Hebrew yathar (H3498) — to remain over; the root of the doctrine of the remnant.

Greek kataleipo (G2641) — to leave behind; the Septuagint and New Testament rendering of Gen 2:24 at Mat 19:5 and Eph 5:31.

Heb 13:5 — a double negative of unusual force in the Greek, piling negatives to say I will not, not ever, leave thee nor forsake thee.

Usage

"“Shall a man leave his father and his mother” — leave, cleave, one flesh, in that order."

"“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” — produced in Scripture as the cure for covetousness."

"“Leave there thy gift before the altar” — reconciliation before ritual."
